excerpt: High-speed burnishing is the cheapest floor-care task per square foot, but minimum charges, machine type and prep work decide what you actually pay. This guide lays out national US unit rates for electric and propane burnishing, per-hour pricing and the minimums that dominate small jobs.
quickAnswer: Nationally, high-speed burnishing costs about $0.015–$0.03 per sq ft per pass when it is added to an existing janitorial route, and $0.03–$0.06 per sq ft as a standalone visit. Hourly billing runs $55–$95 per technician hour, and most vendors apply a $90–$135 per-visit minimum, rising to $175–$300 when a dedicated truck and propane machine must be mobilized. Propane units become the cheaper option above roughly 15,000 sq ft of open hard floor.

blocks.text: What You Are Paying For in a Burnishing Visit

High-speed burnishing polishes an existing floor finish with a pad spinning at 1,500–3,000 rpm. The heat and friction smooth micro-scratches and restore gloss on VCT, LVT with a finish coat, sealed terrazzo and some sealed concrete. It does not remove embedded soil or add finish, so the floor has to be dust mopped and damp mopped first. A quoted burnish price therefore bundles three things: prep (dust mop and damp mop or auto-scrub), the burnish pass itself, and a final dust mop to pick up powder.

Machine choice drives productivity. A 20-inch corded electric burnisher at 1,500–2,000 rpm typically covers 6,000–9,000 sq ft per hour in a real office with doors and corners. A battery burnisher is similar but avoids cord management. A 24- to 27-inch propane burnisher at 2,000–3,000 rpm can cover 12,000–20,000 sq ft per hour in open corridors and lobbies, but it requires emissions controls, ventilation and carbon monoxide monitoring, and many occupied buildings ban it outright.

blocks.text: Burnishing is not priced per fixture the way restroom service is billed at $15–$30 per restroom visit. When a proposal shows per-zone or per-lobby pricing, convert it back to per sq ft to compare against other bids. A $55 elevator lobby charge on 600 sq ft is $0.09 per sq ft, which is high per foot but reasonable once the minimum and prep are counted.
Monthly costs use the industry convention of 4.33 weeks per month, so weekly service equals 4.33 visits and biweekly service equals 2.17 visits. Here is how three common office profiles price out.

items: Small suite, 2,000 sq ft of VCT, burnished biweekly as a route add-on: 2,000 x $0.03 = $60 per visit, but the $90–$135 minimum applies, so the monthly cost is 2.17 x $90–$135 = about $195–$293.
Mid-size office, 8,000 sq ft of VCT, burnished weekly on the nightly route with an electric machine: 8,000 x $0.02–$0.03 = $160–$240 per visit, or 4.33 x that = about $693–$1,039 per month.
Large floor plate, 30,000 sq ft of corridors and lobbies, burnished weekly with propane: 30,000 x $0.015–$0.025 = $450–$750 per visit, or about $1,949–$3,248 per month.
Same 30,000 sq ft burnished with electric machines because the landlord bans propane: 30,000 x $0.02–$0.03 = $600–$900 per visit, or about $2,598–$3,897 per month, roughly 20%–33% more.

blocks.title: Sanity check against labor
blocks.text: At $55 per hour and 8,000 sq ft per hour, raw burnish labor is under $0.01 per sq ft. Prep mopping, pad consumption at roughly one pad per 15,000–25,000 sq ft, travel and machine amortization bring a fair add-on price to $0.02–$0.03. A bid above $0.06 per sq ft on a large open floor deserves a question.
Propane vs Electric: When Each Makes Financial Sense

Propane wins on speed and gloss because the higher pad speed generates more heat. Above about 15,000 sq ft of contiguous hard floor, that speed offsets fuel, cylinder exchange and the extra maintenance on the engine. Below that size, electric machines are usually cheaper because setup time dominates and cord or battery units are already on most janitorial trucks. Propane is also tied to compliance cost: the unit should carry an emissions-certified engine, the operator should be trained on cylinder handling, and the building should have adequate ventilation with a CO monitor clipped to the operator.

blocks.title: Propane indoor air rules
blocks.text: OSHA sets a carbon monoxide permissible exposure limit of 50 ppm averaged over eight hours. Reputable contractors run propane burnishers only in unoccupied, ventilated spaces, carry personal CO monitors, store cylinders outside the building, and document engine tune-ups. Ask for that documentation before approving propane work in a multi-tenant building.
What Raises or Lowers Your Unit Price

Unit rates move with the hard-floor share of your space, the condition of the finish and the access window. A floor with fresh finish burnishes beautifully in one pass; a floor with worn, soft or residue-laden finish can turn gray or swirl under a burnisher and may need a spray-buff or scrub-and-recoat first. Narrow private-office layouts slow the machine and require edge work by hand. Tight access windows, security escorts and elevator holds add idle time that is billed whether or not the machine is running.

Small supplies matter too. Prep quality determines whether the burnish shines or smears. Crews that wipe baseboards and kick plates with color-coded microfiber cloths, such as the Rubbermaid HYGEN damp/wet cloths rated for 500 commercial launderings, and sweep elevator tracks and corners with a flagged-bristle angle broom like the O-Cedar MaxiClean with lobby pan, remove the grit that would otherwise be thrown by the pad. Four-sided 36-inch cones, such as the Rubbermaid bilingual wet floor cone, should mark every damp-mopped lane before the burnisher follows.
How to Request a Comparable Burnishing Quote

items.name: State net hard-floor square footage
items.text: Exclude carpet and list lobbies, corridors, breakrooms and restroom approaches separately.

items.name: Specify the machine constraint
items.text: Tell bidders whether propane is allowed, whether battery is required, and where outlets are available.

items.name: Define the prep standard
items.text: Require dust mop, damp mop with neutral cleaner and a final dust pass so every bid includes the same labor.

items.name: Ask for unit, hourly and minimum
items.text: Request a per sq ft rate, a fallback hourly rate and the per-visit minimum in writing.

items.name: Set the frequency on the 4.33 basis
items.text: State visits per week so monthly totals across bids are calculated the same way.

faqs.q: Is high-speed burnishing priced per square foot or per hour?
faqs.a: Both are common. Route add-ons are usually quoted per sq ft at about $0.015–$0.03, while one-off or project visits may be quoted hourly at $55–$95 per technician hour. Whichever model you accept, confirm the per-visit minimum, typically $90–$135, because it overrides the unit rate on small floors.

faqs.q: Why do some vendors refuse to use propane burnishers in my building?
faqs.a: Propane engines produce carbon monoxide. OSHA limits CO exposure to 50 ppm over an eight-hour shift, and many landlords prohibit propane equipment in occupied or poorly ventilated buildings. A responsible vendor will run propane only after hours with ventilation, personal CO monitors and outdoor cylinder storage, or will switch to battery machines at a modestly higher unit price.

faqs.q: What should a burnishing contract exclude?
faqs.a: Typical exclusions are carpet, unsealed concrete, natural stone that needs diamond polishing, furniture moving beyond chairs and small items, and restorative work such as scrub-and-recoat or strip-and-refinish. Get the exclusion list in writing and ask for unit prices on each excluded task so change orders are predictable.

faqs.q: Do I need a certificate of insurance for a burnishing vendor?
faqs.a: Yes. Request a COI showing general liability, workers compensation and auto coverage for the truck that transports equipment, with your company and landlord named as additional insureds if required by the lease. Crews handling floor chemicals should also have OSHA Hazard Communication training and Safety Data Sheets on site.

faqs.q: How do I convert weekly burnishing into a monthly cost?
faqs.a: Multiply the per-visit price by 4.33. A $240 weekly burnish costs about $1,039 per month, and a biweekly schedule uses 2.17 visits, so the same $240 visit costs about $521 per month.
